claim: NCS-1 and Ric-8A coregulate synapse number and probability of neurotransmitter release.
source: The neuronal calcium sensor 1 (NCS-1), an EF-hand Ca2+ binding protein, and Ric-8A coregulate synapse number and probability of neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation to prior work (Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Structures of Ric-8A bound to Gα have revealed how Ric-8A phosphorylation promotes Gα recognition and activity as a chaperone and guanine nucleotide exchange factor.
source: Recently, the structures of Ric-8A bound to Gα have revealed how Ric-8A phosphorylation promotes Gα recognition and activity as a chaperone and guanine nucleotide exchange factor.
evidence: This claim references recent structural studies that are cited in the manuscript.

claim: The binding of NCS-1 and Gα to Ric-8A are mutually exclusive.
source: Our data show that the binding of NCS-1 and Gα to Ric-8A are mutually exclusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including co-immunoprecipitation and structural studies.

claim: NCS-1 induces a structural rearrangement in Ric-8A that traps the protein in a conformational state that is inaccessible to casein kinase II-mediated phosphorylation.
source: Importantly, NCS-1 induces a structural rearrangement in Ric-8A that traps the protein in a conformational state that is inaccessible to casein kinase II-mediated phosphorylation, demonstrating one aspect of its negative regulation of Ric-8A-mediated G-protein signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by phosphorylation assays and structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NCS-1 complexed with Ric-8A shows a loss of Ric-8A guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity toward Gα.
source: Functional experiments indicate a loss of Ric-8A guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity toward Gα when complexed with NCS-1, and restoration of nucleotide exchange activity upon increasing Ca2+ concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing Ca2+ concentration restores Ric-8A nucleotide exchange activity when complexed with NCS-1.
source: Functional experiments indicate a loss of Ric-8A guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity toward Gα when complexed with NCS-1, and restoration of nucleotide exchange activity upon increasing Ca2+ concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assays at varying Ca2+ concentrations.

claim: NCS-1 is the most abundant protein of the NCS family.
source: The most abundant protein of the NCS family is the neuronal calcium sensor 1 (NCS-1), which was first discovered in Drosophila and named frequenin (Frq), is N-terminally myristoylated (Myr) and highly conserved from yeast to humans (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Pongs et al., 1993; Ames and Lim, 2012; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 was first discovered in Drosophila and named frequenin (Frq).
source: The most abundant protein of the NCS family is the neuronal calcium sensor 1 (NCS-1), which was first discovered in Drosophila and named frequenin (Frq), is N-terminally myristoylated (Myr) and highly conserved from yeast to humans (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Pongs et al., 1993; Ames and Lim, 2012; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 is N-terminally myristoylated.
source: The most abundant protein of the NCS family is the neuronal calcium sensor 1 (NCS-1), which was first discovered in Drosophila and named frequenin (Frq), is N-terminally myristoylated (Myr) and highly conserved from yeast to humans (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Pongs et al., 1993; Ames and Lim, 2012; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 is highly conserved from yeast to humans.
source: The most abundant protein of the NCS family is the neuronal calcium sensor 1 (NCS-1), which was first discovered in Drosophila and named frequenin (Frq), is N-terminally myristoylated (Myr) and highly conserved from yeast to humans (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Pongs et al., 1993; Ames and Lim, 2012; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 is found outside the nervous system.
source: Unlike other NCSs, NCS-1 is found outside the nervous system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 does not contain a Ca2+/Myr switch.
source: It does not contain a Ca2+/Myr switch, thus being constantly bound to the membrane, and has multiple binding partners (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Ames and Lim, 2012; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012; Mansilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 is constantly bound to the membrane.
source: It does not contain a Ca2+/Myr switch, thus being constantly bound to the membrane, and has multiple binding partners (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Ames and Lim, 2012; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012; Mansilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and is inferred from the absence of a Ca2+/Myr switch.

claim: NCS-1 has multiple binding partners.
source: It does not contain a Ca2+/Myr switch, thus being constantly bound to the membrane, and has multiple binding partners (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Ames and Lim, 2012; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012; Mansilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 is a regulator of Ca2+ channels, exocytosis, synaptogenesis, and axonal growth.
source: NCS-1 participates in a wide range of important neuronal functions: it is a regulator of Ca2+ channels, exocytosis, synaptogenesis, and axonal growth, affecting higher functions such as learning and memory, neuroprotection, and axonal regeneration (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012; McFerran et al., 1999; Hui and Feng, 2008; Weiss et al., 2010; Dason et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 affects learning and memory, neuroprotection, and axonal regeneration.
source: NCS-1 participates in a wide range of important neuronal functions: it is a regulator of Ca2+ channels, exocytosis, synaptogenesis, and axonal growth, affecting higher functions such as learning and memory, neuroprotection, and axonal regeneration (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Burgoyne and Haynes, 2012; McFerran et al., 1999; Hui and Feng, 2008; Weiss et al., 2010; Dason et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 has been implicated in X-linked mental retardation and autism, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder.
source: Furthermore, NCS-1 has been implicated in several pathological processes such as X-linked mental retardation and autism, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder (Piton et al., 2008; Koh et al., 2003; Torres et al., 2009; Bahi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The structure of NCS-1 consists of two pairs of EF-hand motifs, of which only three are functional: EF-2, EF-3, and EF-4.
source: The structure of NCS-1 consists of two pairs of EF-hand motifs, of which only three are functional: EF-2, EF-3, and EF-4 (Bourne et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: EF-2 and EF-3 of NCS-1 can recognize Mg2+ as well as Ca2+.
source: EF-2 and EF-3 can recognize Mg2+ as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The two Ca2+/Mg2+ binding sites (EF-2 and EF-3) are structural sites that allow NCS-1 to adopt its tertiary fold.
source: It is known that the two Ca2+/Mg2+ binding sites are structural sites that allow the protein to adopt its tertiary fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and established knowledge.

claim: EF-4 of NCS-1 has been suggested to be a regulatory Ca2+ binding site, able to sense changes in cytosolic calcium levels in neurons.
source: EF-4 has been suggested to be a regulatory Ca2+ binding site, able to sense changes in cytosolic calcium levels in neurons (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Aravind et al., 2008; Mikhaylova et al., 2009; Chandra et al., 2011; Tsvetkov et al., 2018; da Silva et al., 1995; Gifford et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS proteins use a surface-exposed hydrophobic crevice to recognize their targets.
source: The structures of several NCS proteins bound to their corresponding targets have shown that these Ca2+ sensors use a surface-exposed hydrophobic crevice to recognize their targets, which generally present short helical motifs that bind to the N- or C-terminal part of this large cavity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from prior studies and Figure 1A.

claim: NCS protein targets generally present short helical motifs that bind to the N- or C-terminal part of the hydrophobic crevice.
source: The structures of several NCS proteins bound to their corresponding targets have shown that these Ca2+ sensors use a surface-exposed hydrophobic crevice to recognize their targets, which generally present short helical motifs that bind to the N- or C-terminal part of this large cavity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from prior studies and Figure 1A.

claim: The structural determinants of target specificity in NCS proteins are based on the shape and size of the hydrophobic crevice.
source: It has been proposed that the structural determinants of target specificity are based on the shape and size of the hydrophobic crevice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS proteins contain a dynamic C-terminal helix (helix H10) that can insert into the hydrophobic crevice, contributing to its shape.
source: NCS proteins contain a dynamic C-terminal helix (the so-called helix H10) that can insert into the crevice, thus contributing to its shape (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from prior studies and Figure 1A.

claim: Ca2+ binding promotes structural rearrangements in NCS proteins.
source: Since Ca2+ binding promotes structural rearrangements (Figure 1A), the occupancy of the three Ca2+ binding sites also determines affinity for protein partners.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from prior studies and Figure 1A.

claim: The occupancy of the three Ca2+ binding sites in NCS-1 determines affinity for protein partners.
source: Since Ca2+ binding promotes structural rearrangements (Figure 1A), the occupancy of the three Ca2+ binding sites also determines affinity for protein partners.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and inference from Ca2+ binding effects.

claim: Hydrophilic residues at the border of the NCS-1 hydrophobic crevice contribute to target specificity and constitute hot spots for interactions with different targets.
source: Also, the presence of hydrophilic residues at the border of the crevice contributes to target specificity and they constitute hot spots for interactions with the different targets (Burgoyne et al., 2019; Mansilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 is an important regulator of G-protein signaling.
source: Interestingly, NCS-1 is an important regulator of G-protein signaling since it binds to proteins such as GPCRs including the dopamine D2, adenosine 2A, and cannabinoid CB1 receptors (Kabbani et al., 2002; Navarro et al., 2012; Pandalaneni et al., 2015; Angelats et al., 2018); and the molecular chaperone and GEF Ric-8A (Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NCS-1 binds to GPCRs including the dopamine D2, adenosine 2A, and cannabinoid CB1 receptors.
source: Interestingly, NCS-1 is an important regulator of G-protein signaling since it binds to proteins such as GPCRs including the dopamine D2, adenosine 2A, and cannabinoid CB1 receptors (Kabbani et al., 2002; Navarro et al., 2012; Pandalaneni et al., 2015; Angelats et al., 2018); and the molecular chaperone and GEF Ric-8A (Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The NCS-1/Ric-8A complex is implicated in the regulation of synapse number and probability of neurotransmitter release.
source: Although little is known of the regulatory activity of NCS-1 on GPCR function and the cellular and physiological consequences, Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014, showed that the NCS-1/Ric-8A complex is implicated in the regulation of synapse number and probability of neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of the NCS-1/Ric-8A complex formation reduces synapse number and improves learning in Fragile X syndrome animal models.
source: In neurodevelopmental disorders, where synapse number is abnormally high, the inhibition of the NCS-1/Ric-8A complex formation reduces synapse number and improves learning in Fragile X syndrome animal models (Cogram et al., 2022; Mansilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Stabilization of the NCS-1/Ric-8A complex prevents synapse loss and impairment in locomotion in a Drosophila model of Alzheimer's disease neurodegeneration.
source: In contrast, the stabilization of the PPI prevents synapse loss and the consequent impairment in locomotion in a Drosophila model of Alzheimer's disease neurodegeneration at the motor neurons (Canal-Martín et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ric-8A is a ubiquitously expressed cytosolic protein.
source: Ric-8A is an ubiquitously expressed cytosolic protein with two main functions: it constitutes a molecular chaperone that allows heterotrimeric Gα subunit biogenesis (Gabay et al., 2011) and additionally, works as a guanine exchange factor for Gi, Gq, and G12/13 families (Tall et al., 2003; Chan et al., 2011; Van Eps et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ric-8A constitutes a molecular chaperone that allows heterotrimeric Gα subunit biogenesis.
source: Ric-8A is an ubiquitously expressed cytosolic protein with two main functions: it constitutes a molecular chaperone that allows heterotrimeric Gα subunit biogenesis (Gabay et al., 2011) and additionally, works as a guanine exchange factor for Gi, Gq, and G12/13 families (Tall et al., 2003; Chan et al., 2011; Van Eps et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ric-8A works as a guanine exchange factor for Gi, Gq, and G12/13 families.
source: Ric-8A is an ubiquitously expressed cytosolic protein with two main functions: it constitutes a molecular chaperone that allows heterotrimeric Gα subunit biogenesis (Gabay et al., 2011) and additionally, works as a guanine exchange factor for Gi, Gq, and G12/13 families (Tall et al., 2003; Chan et al., 2011; Van Eps et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both chaperone and GEF activities of Ric-8A are stimulated by casein kinase II (CK2) phosphorylation.
source: Both activities are stimulated by casein kinase II (CK2) phosphorylation (Papasergi-Scott et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ric-8A has been shown to regulate asymmetric cell division and is essential for embryonic development.
source: Ric-8A has been shown to regulate asymmetric cell division and is essential for embryonic development (Miller and Rand, 2000; Afshar et al., 2004; Couwenbergs et al., 2004; Tõnissoo et al., 2010; Woodard et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Work in Drosophila has shown the relevance of Ric-8A in activating Gs for in vivo synaptogenesis.
source: Work in Drosophila has shown the relevance of Ric-8A in activating Gs for in vivo synaptogenesis and that this activity is downregulated by NCS-1 (Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ric-8A activity in activating Gs for synaptogenesis is downregulated by NCS-1.
source: Work in Drosophila has shown the relevance of Ric-8A in activating Gs for in vivo synaptogenesis and that this activity is downregulated by NCS-1 (Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ric-8A residues S435 and T440 stabilizes a conformation that is competent for Gα recognition.
source: These works revealed the structural basis of Ric-8A as a Gα chaperone and GEF and showed how phosphorylation of Ric-8A residues S435 and T440 stabilizes a conformation that is competent for Gα recognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: Based on genetic studies, it has been proposed that NCS-1 interacts with Ric-8A and prevents the Ric-8A/Gα interaction.
source: Based on genetic studies, it has been proposed that NCS-1 interacts with Ric-8A and prevents the Ric-8A/Gα interaction (Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior genetic studies.

claim: The HEAT repeat 9 of Ric-8A, composed of a two-helix bundle (a9 and b9), has marked hydrophobic character.
source: Using these criteria, we evaluated the hydrophobic character of the HEAT repeat 9 of the ARM/HEAT repeat domain of Ric-8A, which is composed of a two-helix bundle (called a9 and b9), as well as two C-terminal helical motifs (rH10 and rH11), all of them involved in Gα recognition (Figure 1B). The marked hydrophobic character of the a9-b9 two-helix bundle led us to hypothesize that a9 and/or b9 helices could be implicated in the interaction with NCS-1.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of structural data and is supported by Figure 1B.

claim: The a9 and/or b9 helices of Ric-8A could be implicated in the interaction with NCS-1.
source: The marked hydrophobic character of the a9-b9 two-helix bundle led us to hypothesize that a9 and/or b9 helices could be implicated in the interaction with NCS-1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: The NCS-1 C-terminal helix H10 works as a built-in competitive inhibitor of the Ric-8A interaction.
source: The NCS-1 C-terminal helix H10 was removed since it works as a built-in competitive inhibitor of the Ric-8A interaction and the affinity for Ric-8A increases 30% in the absence of this helix (Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The affinity of NCS-1 for Ric-8A increases 30% in the absence of helix H10.
source: The NCS-1 C-terminal helix H10 was removed since it works as a built-in competitive inhibitor of the Ric-8A interaction and the affinity for Ric-8A increases 30% in the absence of this helix (Romero-Pozuelo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Neither a Ca2+-free nor a fully Ca2+-loaded NCS-1 protein recognized Ric-8A properly.
source: Therefore, neither a Ca2+-free nor a fully Ca2+-loaded NCS-1 protein recognized Ric-8A properly, suggesting that Ca2+ loading of some, out of the 3 Ca2+ binding sites, is required for Ric-8A recognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by assembly experiments presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Ca2+ loading of some, but not all, of the 3 Ca2+ binding sites of NCS-1 is required for Ric-8A recognition.
source: Therefore, neither a Ca2+-free nor a fully Ca2+-loaded NCS-1 protein recognized Ric-8A properly, suggesting that Ca2+ loading of some, out of the 3 Ca2+ binding sites, is required for Ric-8A recognition.
evidence: This claim is inferred from assembly experiments presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The majority of the NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452 protein sample eluted at an apparent molecular mass consistent with the formation of the complex when assembled by dialysis from EGTA to Ca2+.
source: The majority of the protein sample eluted at an apparent molecular mass consistent with the formation of the NCS-1ΔH10/Ric-8A complex, as confirmed by SDS-PAGE gel (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography and SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nano-DSF experiments corroborated the efficient assembly of NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452 when moving from EGTA to intermediate Ca2+ conditions.
source: Nano-differential scanning fluorimetry (nano-DSF) experiments also corroborated the efficient assembly when moving from EGTA to intermediate Ca2+ conditions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by nano-DSF data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The thermal transition of Ric-8A is up-shifted by more than 20°C (Ti = 79.7 ± 2.8°C) in the NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452 complex due to complex formation promoted by NCS-1 Ca2+ uptake.
source: In contrast, the thermal transition of Ric-8A is up-shifted by more than 20°C (Ti = 79.7 ± 2.8°C) in the sample dialyzed from EGTA to Ca2+ concentrations, due to the complex formation promoted by NCS-1 Ca2+ uptake.
evidence: This claim is supported by nano-DSF data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Ti of the Ca2+-bound form of NCS-1 in the NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452 complex is 82.8 ± 2.6°C, which is significantly lower than when the three Ca2+ binding sites are saturated (above 90°C).
source: Moreover, the Ti of the Ca2+-bound form of NCS-1 in the sample is 82.8 ± 2.6°C, a value that is significantly lower than that shown when the three Ca2+ binding sites are saturated, which is above 90°C (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by nano-DSF data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The non-phosphorylatable version of hRic-8A (S436A, T441A) retains its ability to interact with hNCS-1.
source: The co-immunoprecipitation of the protein complex shows that the non-phosphorylatable version of hRic-8A retains its ability to interact with hNCS-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The binding of the non-phosphorylatable hRic-8A (S436A, T441A) to hNCS-1 is increased with respect to the wild-type version.
source: Interestingly, the binding is increased with respect to the wild-type version, which would suggest that Ric-8A is partly phosphorylated in vivo and this might hinder the interaction with NCS-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ric-8A is partly phosphorylated in vivo, which might hinder the interaction with NCS-1.
source: Interestingly, the binding is increased with respect to the wild-type version, which would suggest that Ric-8A is partly phosphorylated in vivo and this might hinder the interaction with NCS-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased binding of the non-phosphorylatable mutant to NCS-1.

claim: Uncomplexed rRic-8A-452 is phosphorylated after CK2 treatment.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, while uncomplexed rRic-8A-452 is phosphorylated after CK2 treatment, rRic-8A-452 is not phosphorylated when complexed with NCS-1, since the anionic exchange elution profile of the NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452 complex is the same regardless of CK2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by anion exchange chromatography data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: rRic-8A-452 is not phosphorylated when complexed with NCS-1.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, while uncomplexed rRic-8A-452 is phosphorylated after CK2 treatment, rRic-8A-452 is not phosphorylated when complexed with NCS-1, since the anionic exchange elution profile of the NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452 complex is the same regardless of CK2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by anion exchange chromatography and LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No phosphopeptides were found in NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452 complex after CK2 treatment, even with phosphopeptide enrichment.
source: To further verify the phosphorylation state of Ric-8A in the CK2-treated samples, we used LC-MS/MS with the aim of identifying phosphopeptides from a trypsin-digested sample (see Materials and methods). While phosphopeptides were found in the rRic-8A-452 control sample (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) no phosphopeptides were found in NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452, even though a phosphopeptide enrichment protocol was performed, supporting the hypothesis that the binding of NCS-1 precludes CK2-mediated phosphorylation of Ric-8A.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The binding of NCS-1 precludes CK2-mediated phosphorylation of Ric-8A.
source: While phosphopeptides were found in the rRic-8A-452 control sample (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) no phosphopeptides were found in NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452, even though a phosphopeptide enrichment protocol was performed, supporting the hypothesis that the binding of NCS-1 precludes CK2-mediated phosphorylation of Ric-8A.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS and anion exchange chromatography data.

claim: Phosphorylated rRic-8A-452 does not efficiently interact with NCS-1ΔH10.
source: Finally, we asked whether phosphorylated Ric-8A can interact with NCS-1. An assembly experiment was performed similarly to that described for the unphosphorylated protein (control). Our data show that phosphorylated rRic-8A-452 does not efficiently interact with NCS-1ΔH10 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, Ric-8A-491 increases the rate of nucleotide exchange at ΔN31Gαi1 almost fourfold over the intrinsic rate.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, Ric-8A-491 increases the rate of nucleotide exchange at ΔN31Gαi1 almost fourfold over the intrinsic rate, whereas His-NCS-1/Ric-8A-491 does not significantly affect the exchange rate (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: His-NCS-1/Ric-8A-491 does not significantly affect the nucleotide exchange rate at ΔN31Gαi1 in the absence of Ca2+.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, Ric-8A-491 increases the rate of nucleotide exchange at ΔN31Gαi1 almost fourfold over the intrinsic rate, whereas His-NCS-1/Ric-8A-491 does not significantly affect the exchange rate (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ca2+ increases the intrinsic and Ric-8A-catalyzed rates of nucleotide exchange at ΔN31Gαi1 in equal measure.
source: We found that Ca2+ increases the intrinsic and Ric-8A-catalyzed rates of nucleotide exchange at ΔN31Gαi1 in equal measure (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ca2+ produces a concentration-dependent enhancement of the nucleotide exchange rate in the presence of His-NCS-1/Ric-8A-491.
source: However, after correcting for this effect, it is evident that Ca2+ produces a concentration-dependent enhancement of the exchange rate in the presence of His-NCS-1/Ric-8A-491 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At 25 µM CaCl2, ~35% of the nucleotide exchange rate is restored to levels similar to that observed in the presence of Ric-8A-491 alone.
source: At 25 µM CaCl2, ~35% of the nucleotide exchange rate is restored to levels similar to that observed in the presence of Ric-8A-491 alone (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NCS-1 complexed to Ric-8A effectively inhibits the GEF activity of Ric-8A.
source: Thus, NCS-1 complexed to Ric-8A effectively inhibits the GEF activity of Ric-8A whereas addition of CaCl2 restores GEF activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Addition of CaCl2 restores GEF activity of Ric-8A when complexed with NCS-1.
source: Thus, NCS-1 complexed to Ric-8A effectively inhibits the GEF activity of Ric-8A whereas addition of CaCl2 restores GEF activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The apparent activation constant for Ca2+-induced enhancement of the intrinsic and Ric-8A-catalyzed nucleotide exchange rates at ΔN31Gαi1 is Ka-EXC=29 ± 8 µM.
source: From these data, it is possible to calculate the apparent activation constant for Ca2+-induced enhancement of the intrinsic and Ric-8A-catalyzed nucleotide exchange rates at ΔN31Gαi1 (Ka-EXC=29 ± 8 µM, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data and fitting shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Ca2+-induced apparent activation constant for its action on the NCS-1/Ric-8A complex is Ka-NCS-1=61 ± 35 µM.
source: In addition, it is possible to estimate a Ca2+-induced apparent activation constant for its action on the NCS-1/Ric-8A complex, which disassembles upon Ca2+ binding to NCS-1 EF-4, enabling Ric-8A to catalyze Gαi1 nucleotide exchange (Ka-NCS-1=61 ± 35 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide exchange assay data and fitting.

claim: The HEAT repeat 9 of Ric-8A undergoes a substantial conformational change upon binding to NCS-1: helix a9 unfolds while helix b9 refolds, resulting in regions R1 and R2.
source: As shown by the crystal structures presented here, the HEAT repeat 9 undergoes a substantial conformational change: helix a9 unfolds while helix b9 refolds, resulting in the named regions R1 and R2 (Figure 3B and Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figures 3B and 7B.

claim: The relative orientation of R1 and R2 change with respect to a9 and b9 upon NCS-1 binding.
source: The relative orientation of R1 and R2 change with respect to a9 and b9.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: If helices b9 and R2 are superposed, helix a9 is rotated ~180 degrees with respect to R1.
source: If helices b9 and R2 are superposed, helix a9 is rotated ~180 degrees with respect to R1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the Ric-8A/Gα complex, hydrophobic residues in the HEAT repeat 9 are facing the ARM repeat 8 to create contacts between the two repeats.
source: In the Ric-8A/Gα complex, hydrophobic residues in the HEAT repeat 9 are facing the ARM repeat 8 to create contacts between the two repeats (Figure 7A and C and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7A and C and Video 1.

claim: In the NCS-1ΔH10/Ric-8A-P complex, hydrophobic residues of Ric-8A are exposed to the solvent, affording their interaction with the hydrophobic crevice of NCS-1.

source: The fact that the NCS-1 Ca2+ and structural determinants are different in recognizing Ric-8A and the dopamine D2 receptor is conceptually relevant, since opens the path to the design of selective drugs that target specifically these neuronal pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The difference in NCS-1 Ca2+ and structural determinants for recognizing Ric-8A and the dopamine D2 receptor opens the path to the design of selective drugs that target specifically these neuronal pathways.
source: The fact that the NCS-1 Ca2+ and structural determinants are different in recognizing Ric-8A and the dopamine D2 receptor is conceptually relevant, since opens the path to the design of selective drugs that target specifically these neuronal pathways.

claim: Human full-length NCS-1 has 100% protein sequence identity with the rat variant.
source: Human full-length NCS-1 (100% protein sequence identity with the rat variant) was cloned in the pETDuet vector (Canal-Martín et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The three Ca2+ binding sites of NCS-1, EF-2, EF-3, and EF-4, are occupied in the hNCS-1ΔH10/Ric-8A-P complexes, showing a pentagonal-bipyramidal coordination.
source: The analysis of the structure of the hNCS-1ΔH10/Ric-8A-P complexes presented in this work, together with electron density map calculations, indicate that the three Ca2+ binding sites, EF-2, EF-3, and EF-4, are occupied, showing a pentagonal-bipyramidal coordination (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The anomalous difference map shows 6σ peaks at EF-2 and EF-3 metal sites while no signal is observed in EF-4, indicating unambiguously the presence of Ca2+ at sites EF-2 and EF-3.
source: The anomalous difference map shows 6σ peaks at EF-2 and EF-3 metal sites while no signal is observed in EF-4, indicating unambiguously the presence of Ca2+ at sites EF-2 and EF-3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anomalous difference map data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EF-4 shows a residual anomalous signal when reducing the σ level, which could indicate a low occupancy of Ca2+ at EF-4.
source: EF-4 shows a residual anomalous signal when reducing the σ level, which could indicate a low occupancy of Ca2+ at EF-4, consistent with the observation that a fully saturated NCS-1 does not recognize Ric-8A properly (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by anomalous difference map data and assembly data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EF-4 of NCS-1 is unable to bind Mg2+.
source: We have not modeled Mg2+ at any of the metal binding sites since it has been reported that EF-4 is unable to bind this metal (Aravind et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A Na+ ion was modeled at EF-4 of NCS-1 in the crystal structure.
source: Taking these observations together, a Na+ ion was modeled at EF-4 (Figure 4A), since Na+ was present in the crystallization solution, does not scatter X-rays anomalously, and is structurally undistinguishable from Ca2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and reasoning presented in the manuscript.

claim: Na+ was present in the crystallization solution.
source: Taking these observations together, a Na+ ion was modeled at EF-4 (Figure 4A), since Na+ was present in the crystallization solution, does not scatter X-rays anomalously, and is structurally undistinguishable from Ca2+.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Na+ does not scatter X-rays anomalously.
source: Taking these observations together, a Na+ ion was modeled at EF-4 (Figure 4A), since Na+ was present in the crystallization solution, does not scatter X-rays anomalously, and is structurally undistinguishable from Ca2+.
evidence: This is established knowledge in crystallography.

claim: Na+ is structurally undistinguishable from Ca2+ in X-ray crystallography.
source: Taking these observations together, a Na+ ion was modeled at EF-4 (Figure 4A), since Na+ was present in the crystallization solution, does not scatter X-rays anomalously, and is structurally undistinguishable from Ca2+. Their similar ionic radii allow equivalent heptahedral geometry, distances, and angles (Harding, 2002; Groom et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in crystallography supported by citations.

claim: An increase in Na+ concentration produces an enhancement of the emission fluorescence intensity of full-length hNCS-1 that achieves saturation at 300 mM NaCl.
source: Our data show that an increase in Na+ concentration produces an enhancement of the emission fluorescence intensity that achieves saturation at 300 mM NaCl.
evidence: This claim is supported by tryptophan emission fluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The apparent dissociation constant of NCS-1 for Na+ is 123.4±26.6 mM.
source: Considering a 1:1 equilibrium, it is possible to estimate the apparent dissociation constant from these data, which is 123.4±26.6 mM (Mansilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by tryptophan emission fluorescence data and fitting.

claim: The addition of K+ to NCS-1 promotes smaller changes in the emission intensity compared to Na+, which varied linearly with the cation concentration up to 500 mM KCl, with no sign of saturation.
source: Compared with Na+, the addition of K+ promotes smaller changes in the emission intensity, which varied linearly with the cation concentration up to 500 mM KCl, with no sign of saturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by tryptophan emission fluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: NCS-1 is unable to bind K+ at physiologically relevant concentrations.
source: This suggests that NCS-1 is unable to bind K+ at physiologically relevant concentrations (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from the tryptophan emission fluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The tryptophan emission fluorescence experiments support the binding of Na+ to NCS-1.
source: Therefore, the tryptophan emission fluorescence experiments support the binding of Na+ to NCS-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by tryptophan emission fluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The changes observed upon Na+ binding to NCS-1 may reflect variations in the environment of W103 (EF-3 helix H6), which is the tryptophan residue closer to the EF-4 Na+ binding site.
source: The changes observed upon Na+ binding may reflect variations in the environment of W103 (EF-3 helix H6), which is the tryptophan residue closer to the EF-4 Na+ binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and the location of W103.

claim: The EF-4 helix H9 is connected to EF-3 helix H6 through multiple hydrophobic contacts.
source: In fact, the EF-4 helix H9 is connected to EF-3 helix H6 through multiple hydrophobic contacts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), so that the structural rearrangement that occurs upon Na+ binding at EF-4 could be transmitted to W103.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The structural rearrangement that occurs upon Na+ binding at EF-4 could be transmitted to W103.
source: In fact, the EF-4 helix H9 is connected to EF-3 helix H6 through multiple hydrophobic contacts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), so that the structural rearrangement that occurs upon Na+ binding at EF-4 could be transmitted to W103.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: EF-hand motifs always occur in pairs and upon Ca2+ binding, EF-hands communicate with each other through the Ca2+ binding loops and helix-helix contacts, in order to orchestrate structural rearrangement and transmit the Ca2+ signal.
source: Indeed, EF-hand motifs always occur in pairs and upon Ca2+ binding, EF-hands communicate with each other through the Ca2+ binding loops and helix-helix contacts, in order to orchestrate structural rearrangement and transmit the Ca2+ signal (Grabarek, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Na+ binding to a Ca2+ binding loop is transmitted between EF-hands.
source: Here, we show that Na+ binding to a Ca2+ binding loop is also transmitted between EF-hands.
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented.

claim: The formation of the NCS-1ΔH10/rRic-8A-452 complex is achieved in the presence of either Na+ or K+.
source: The formation of the complex is achieved in the presence of either ion (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by assembly data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Only binding of Ca2+ to the structural sites EF-2 and EF-3 triggers the conformational rearrangement needed for Ric-8A recognition.
source: Therefore, as suggested by the Ca2+ titration experiments (Figure 2A) only binding of Ca2+ to the structural sites EF-2 and EF-3 (Aravind et al., 2008) triggers the conformational rearrangement needed for Ric-8A recognition, and Na+ occupation of EF-4 does not contribute to NCS-1/Ric-8A complex formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the assembly data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4C.

claim: Na+ occupation of EF-4 does not contribute to NCS-1/Ric-8A complex formation.
source: Therefore, as suggested by the Ca2+ titration experiments (Figure 2A) only binding of Ca2+ to the structural sites EF-2 and EF-3 (Aravind et al., 2008) triggers the conformational rearrangement needed for Ric-8A recognition, and Na+ occupation of EF-4 does not contribute to NCS-1/Ric-8A complex formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the assembly data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4C.

claim: Ric-8A can bind to NCS-1 species with a Ca2+-free EF-4 site, and in this situation, at 100 mM Na+ concentrations, the site is occupied with Na+.
source: Therefore, Ric-8A can bind to NCS-1 species with a Ca2+-free EF-4 site, and in this situation, and at the 100 mM Na+ concentrations used in the crystallization conditions, the site is occupied with Na+.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystallographic and assembly data.

claim: In both Na+ and K+ containing media, the binding of Ca2+ to NCS-1 can be fit to a sequential binding model assuming three available sites.
source: In both media the binding data can be fit to a sequential binding model assuming three available sites (Figure 4D), the first and last binding steps being enthalpy-driven and the second step entropy-driven.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The first and last Ca2+ binding steps to NCS-1 are enthalpy-driven and the second step is entropy-driven.
source: In both media the binding data can be fit to a sequential binding model assuming three available sites (Figure 4D), the first and last binding steps being enthalpy-driven and the second step entropy-driven.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Filling of the third Ca2+ binding site of NCS-1 is significantly delayed compared to the occupation of the other two sites.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, filling of the third site is significantly delayed compared to the occupation of the other two sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A previous NMR-based study showed that Ca2+ sequentially binds to EF-2, EF-3, and finally EF-4 of NCS-1, based on the microscopic binding constant measured for each site.
source: However, a previous NMR-based study showed that Ca2+ sequentially binds to EF-2, EF-3, and finally EF-4, based in the microscopic binding constant measured for each site (Aravind et al., 2008; Mikhaylova et al., 2009; Chandra et al., 2011; Tsvetkov et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior NMR studies.

claim: The interaction of NCS-1 with Ca2+ depends on the monovalent cation present in the media.
source: Interestingly, a direct inspection of the isotherms suggests that the interaction with Ca2+ depends on the monovalent cation present in the media.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The dissociation constants of the first and last Ca2+ binding steps to NCS-1 increase by about 1.5 times in the presence of Na+ compared to K+.
source: In particular, we observe that the dissociation constants of the first and last steps (likely involving sites EF-2 and EF-4) increase by about 1.5 times in the presence of Na+, while that of the second step doubles and its enthalpy change triples.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D and Table 4.

claim: The dissociation constant of the second Ca2+ binding step to NCS-1 doubles and its enthalpy change triples in the presence of Na+ compared to K+.
source: In particular, we observe that the dissociation constants of the first and last steps (likely involving sites EF-2 and EF-4) increase by about 1.5 times in the presence of Na+, while that of the second step doubles and its enthalpy change triples.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4D and Table 4.

claim: Na+ binding modulates the affinity of NCS-1 for Ca2+, the influence likely extending to more than one site due to communication among them.
source: In conclusion, our data suggest that Na+ binding modulates the affinity of NCS-1 for Ca2+, the influence likely extending to more than one site due to communication among them (Gifford et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC data.

claim: The possibility that Na+ could bind to more than one unoccupied Ca2+ site of NCS-1 cannot be completely discarded.
source: However, the possibility that Na+ could bind to more than one unoccupied Ca2+ site cannot be completely discarded.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty.

claim: When the regulatory EF-4 Ca2+ binding site of NCS-1 is empty (0 nM Ca2+ and 125 mM Na+ experimental conditions), the apparent dissociation constant of the NCS-1/Ric-8A-P3 complex is in the hundreds of the µM range.
source: Our data show that when the regulatory EF-4 Ca2+ binding site is empty (0 nM Ca2+ and 125 mM Na+ experimental conditions), the apparent dissociation constant of the NCS-1/Ric-8A-P3 complex is in the hundreds of the µM range.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 4E and Table 3.

claim: At 250 nM Ca2+, the affinity of NCS-1 for Ric-8A-P3 is decreased 1.5 times compared to 0 nM Ca2+.
source: However, at high cellular Ca2+ concentrations (250 nM), the affinity is decreased 1.5 times.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 4E and Table 3.

claim: At 425 nM Ca2+, when Ca2+ concentrations are above the Kd of the regulatory EF-4 Ca2+ binding site, NCS-1 affinity for Ric-8A-P3 is greatly reduced to the mM range.
source: At 425 nM Ca2+, when Ca2+ concentrations are above the Kd of the regulatory EF-4 Ca2+ binding site (see Table 4, site 3), NCS-1 affinity for Ric-8A-P3 is greatly reduced to the mM range.
evidence: This claim is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 4E and Table 3.

claim: hRic-8A-424 has significantly higher affinity for NCS-1 compared with hRic-8A-FL.
source: Compared with hRic-8A-FL (Figure 2C), hRic-8A-424 has significantly higher affinity for NCS-1, suggesting that the HEAT repeat 9, but not the rH10 or rH11 helices, is implicated in the PPI.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The HEAT repeat 9 of Ric-8A, but not the rH10 or rH11 helices, is implicated in the interaction with NCS-1.
source: Compared with hRic-8A-FL (Figure 2C), hRic-8A-424 has significantly higher affinity for NCS-1, suggesting that the HEAT repeat 9, but not the rH10 or rH11 helices, is implicated in the PPI.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The hNCS-1ΔH10/Ric-8A-P contact area is 1140 Å2.
source: The hNCS-1ΔH10/Ric-8A-P contact area is 1140 Å2 (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) and a total of 1469 contacts take place (4.2 Å cutoff distance).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: A total of 1469 contacts take place between hNCS-1ΔH10 and Ric-8A-P (4.2 Å cutoff distance).
source: The hNCS-1ΔH10/Ric-8A-P contact area is 1140 Å2 (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007) and a total of 1469 contacts take place (4.2 Å cutoff distance).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: All the NCS-1 helices that shape the cavity are implicated in Ric-8A recognition.
source: All the NCS-1 helices that shape the cavity are implicated in Ric-8A recognition: while R2 helix is recognized by multiple helices, R1 contacts helices H7 and H8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: A total of nine H-bonds are formed between NCS-1 and Ric-8A in the cavity.
source: A total of nine H-bonds are formed with Ric-8A in the cavity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Helix R2 of Ric-8A is recognized by NCS-1 at the middle (L419), N- (N414) and C-terminus (R429) through H-bonds.
source: Helix R2 is recognized at the middle (L419), N- (N414) and C-terminus (R429) through H-bonds.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The Ric-8A R1-R2 loop plays a relevant role in the recognition process and Y412 forms two water-mediated H-bonds with residues located at the C-terminal part of the NCS-1 crevice.
source: The Ric-8A R1-R2 loop also plays a relevant role in the recognition process and Y412 forms two water-mediated H-bonds with residues located at the C-terminal part of the crevice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: NCS-1 residue R148 uses its guanidinium group to establish two direct H-bonds with T410 (R1-R2 loop) and K408 (R2 helix) of Ric-8A.
source: NCS-1 residue R148 uses its guanidinium group to establish two direct H-bonds with T410 (R1-R2 loop) and K408 (R2 helix).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: All NCS-1 residues involved in polar contacts with Ric-8A are located at the border of the hydrophobic crevice in which Ric-8A is inserted.
source: All NCS-1 residues involved in polar contacts are located at the border of the hydrophobic crevice in which Ric-8A is inserted (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A large number of van der Waals interactions are formed between Ric-8A and the bottom and lateral walls of the NCS-1 crevice in which hydrophobic and aromatic residues are present.
source: In addition to the polar contacts, a large number of van der Waals interactions are formed with the bottom and lateral walls of the NCS-1 crevice in which hydrophobic and a good number of aromatic residues are present (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Several hydrophobic and aromatic Ric-8A residues satisfy van der Waals interactions with NCS-1.
source: Several hydrophobic and aromatic Ric-8A residues satisfy these interactions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The region of Ric-8A that is necessary and sufficient for NCS-1 recognition is conserved in rat and human protein sequences.
source: Using Ric-8A peptides of different lengths to generate crystal structures, together with PPI assays, it has been possible to define the region of Ric-8A that is necessary and sufficient for NCS-1 recognition and which is conserved in rat and human protein sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic and co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The addition of three extra residues (peptide P3 vs P2) may allow better folding of the R2 helix of Ric-8A.
source: The addition of three extra residues (peptide P3 vs P2) may allow better folding of the R2 helix.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and PPI assays.

claim: A cell-based PPI assay with an hRic-8A deletion mutant (hRic-8A-433) ending at G432 shows the strongest interaction with full-length hNCS-1.
source: In fact, a cell-based PPI assay with an hRic-8A deletion mutant (hRic-8A-433) ending like rRic-8A-P3 at G432 shows the strongest interaction with full-length hNCS-1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All Ric-8A-P modeled residues except the N-terminal S402, and the residues P404, R405, and F406 are involved in the interaction with NCS-1.
source: The crystal structure shows that all Ric-8A-P modeled residues except the N-terminal S402, and the residues P404, R405, and F406 (which belong to helix R1 and are exposed to the solvent, opposite to the face that contacts NCS-1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D) are involved in the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figures 3—figure supplement 1A, 3B, and 3—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: The long R2 helix of Ric-8A highly contributes to the protein-protein contact area with multiple van der Waals contacts and four H-bonds.
source: The long R2 helix highly contributes to the protein-protein contact area with multiple van der Waals contacts and four H-bonds.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The R1-R2 loop of Ric-8A, formed by residues T410, G411, Y412, and G413, contributes with three hydrogen bonds to the PPI with NCS-1.
source: Shorter regions such as the R1-R2 loop, only formed by residues T410, G411, Y412, and G413, are also implicated in the PPI, contributing with three hydrogen bonds (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The four residues of the R1-R2 loop (T410, G411, Y412, and G413) account for 28% of total contacts between hNCS-1 and Ric-8A-P.
source: In fact, these four residues account for 28% of total contacts between hNCS-1 and Ric-8A-P.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis.

claim: Mutations R148A, R151A in NCS-1 do not alter Ric-8A binding, despite three H-bonds being lost at the bottom of the crevice.
source: The co-immunoprecipitation assays show that mutations R148A, R151A in NCS-1 do not alter Ric-8A binding, despite three H-bonds are lost at the bottom of the crevice.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: When the recognition of Ric-8A R2 helix is affected at the middle and C-terminus of NCS-1 crevice (Y52A and D37A, respectively), differences in binding are not significant.
source: When the recognition of Ric-8A R2 helix is affected at the middle and C-terminus of NCS-1 crevice (Y52A and D37A, respectively), differences in binding are not significant either.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The combination of mutations at the top and bottom of NCS-1 crevice (triple mutant; D37A, R148A, R151A) has a statistically significant impact on the interaction with Ric-8A (40% binding loss).
source: The combination of mutations at the top and bottom of NCS-1 crevice (triple mutant; D37A, R148A, R151A), which would affect the recognition of both Ric-8A helices and the R1-R2 loop, has a statistically significant impact on the interaction (40% binding loss).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The NCS-1 quadruple mutant (D37A, Y52A, R148A, R151A) shows the deepest impact on the interaction with Ric-8A (more than 60% binding loss).
source: As expected, the quadruple mutant (D37A, Y52A, R148A, R151A) shows the deepest impact on the interaction (more than 60% binding loss), since H-bonds are disrupted at the top, middle, and bottom of the PPI.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A Ric-8A triple mutant, T410A, Y412A, N414A, shows no changes in NCS-1 binding.
source: To further understand the relevance of the R1-R2 loop (Table 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D), a Ric-8A triple mutant, T410A, Y412A, N414A (which would correspond to T411A, Y413A, N415A in the human protein), was tested in the PPI binding assay showing no changes in NCS-1 binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutations in NCS-1 W30 (W30A) and two Ric-8A residues close to NCS-1 W30, L424, and M425 (L425 and M426 in the human protein) have a relevant impact on the PPI, reducing binding more than 50%.
source: Mutations include NCS-1 W30 (W30A) and two Ric-8A residues close to NCS-1 W30, L424, and M425 (L425 and M426 in the human protein) (Table 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and D). Despite these residues only mediate long-range hydrophobic contacts, and no H-bond is affected, the impact on the PPI is relevant and binding is reduced more than 50%.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The effect of mutations in NCS-1 W30 and Ric-8A L424, M425 on the PPI is similar to that found when disrupting H-bonds all along the PPI (NCS-1 quadruple mutant).
source: The effect is similar to that found when disrupting H-bonds all along the PPI (NCS-1 quadruple mutant).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.
